standard.name: PEP 8 – Style Guide for Python Code

namingRules.description: Keep module filenames brief and entirely lowercase. An underscore inside the name is fine when it makes a multi-word module easier to read at a glance, but is not required otherwise.
namingRules.rationale: Lowercase module names keep import statements predictable and avoid case-sensitivity issues across filesystems.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Package and Module Names

namingRules.description: Packages follow the same short, all-lowercase style as modules, but underscores are actively avoided at the package level rather than merely optional.
namingRules.rationale: Short, underscore-free package names are easier to type in import paths and match long-standing PyPI conventions.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Package and Module Names

namingRules.description: By default, name a class using the CapWords style: each word capitalized and concatenated without separators (also known as PascalCase).
namingRules.rationale: CapWords visually distinguishes types from functions and variables, which use lowercase conventions.

namingRules.description: Exceptions are named like any other class, in CapWords, with one addition: if the exception actually represents a genuine error state (rather than, say, a control-flow signal), its name should end in 'Error'.
namingRules.rationale: The Error suffix lets readers identify exception types at a glance and distinguishes true errors from control-flow-only exceptions.

namingRules.description: Functions are named in all-lowercase snake_case; insert underscores between words only where doing so makes the name easier to read, since a short function name needs none.
namingRules.rationale: A single consistent case style for callables makes function names instantly recognizable and distinguishes them from class names.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Variable Names

namingRules.description: Method names follow the same lowercase-with-underscores rule as functions.
namingRules.rationale: Applying the function-naming rule uniformly to methods keeps a class's public interface consistent with the rest of the codebase.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

namingRules.description: Variable names follow the same convention as function names: lowercase with underscores separating words.
namingRules.rationale: Uniform casing for variables and functions avoids arbitrary style decisions and keeps identifiers scannable.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Variable Names

namingRules.description: Module-level constants are written entirely in capital letters, with underscores marking the boundaries between words.
namingRules.rationale: All-caps names flag values that are meant to be treated as fixed, reducing accidental reassignment.

namingRules.description: The first parameter of an instance method must always be named 'self'; the first parameter of a class method must always be named 'cls'.
namingRules.rationale: Fixed conventional names for the implicit first argument let readers immediately recognize instance vs. class methods.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Method Arguments

namingRules.description: If the most natural parameter name happens to clash with a Python reserved word, resolve the clash with one trailing underscore on the name rather than misspelling or shortening it.
namingRules.rationale: A trailing underscore keeps the parameter's meaning intact instead of obscuring it with an abbreviation.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Method Arguments

namingRules.description: Instance attributes intended as non-public should carry a single leading underscore; attributes without one are considered part of the public interface.
namingRules.rationale: A single leading underscore is a widely understood, weak 'internal use' signal that documents intent without enforcing access control.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

namingRules.description: A double leading underscore (with no trailing underscore) may be used on an attribute to invoke Python's name-mangling mechanism, helping avoid attribute name clashes when the class is subclassed.
namingRules.rationale: Name mangling is an opt-in mechanism reserved for attributes that genuinely need subclass-clash protection, so it is optional rather than a default rule.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

namingRules.description: Do not choose a bare lowercase L, uppercase O, or uppercase I as a standalone identifier; depending on the font, each can be mistaken for the digit 1 or 0.
namingRules.rationale: Visually ambiguous single-letter names cause misreadings that are hard to catch in code review.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Names to Avoid

namingRules.description: Public instance attributes should be exposed as plain, simply-named attributes with no leading underscore, rather than hidden behind getter/setter accessor methods unless additional behavior is actually needed.
namingRules.rationale: Plain attribute access is more idiomatic and readable in Python; properties can be introduced later without breaking the public interface.
namingRules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Designing for Inheritance

commentRules.triggerCondition: the module is public (not prefixed with an underscore) and forms part of the package's API
commentRules.description: Public modules should have a docstring summarizing their contents. Neither PEP 8 nor PEP 257 mandates a specific docstring markup style (no required Google-, NumPy-, or reST-style sections) — only the high-level convention that it exists and starts with a one-line summary.

Public classes should have a docstring summarizing the class's behavior; PEP 257 additionally suggests listing public methods and instance variables, but prescribes no required markup syntax for how that content is formatted.

Public functions should have a docstring describing their behavior. Per PEP 257 it should cover arguments, return value, side effects, and exceptions where applicable, but no specific markup style (e.g. Google-style Args:/Returns: sections) is mandated by PEP 8 or PEP 257 — the content, not the format, is the requirement.

commentRules.triggerCondition: the method is public; if the method is non-public (leading underscore) a docstring is optional
commentRules.description: Public methods should carry a docstring. Docstrings are not necessary for non-public methods, but PEP 8 recommends at least an explanatory comment describing what a non-public method does.

commentRules.triggerCondition: a block comment precedes a block of code
commentRules.description: Write block comments as full, properly capitalized sentences, prefix each line with a hash and one space, and update them whenever the code they explain changes, since an outdated comment misleads more than an absent one.

commentRules.triggerCondition: an inline comment follows a statement on the same line
commentRules.description: Reserve inline comments for cases that genuinely need them; keep at least two spaces before the hash, follow it with one space, and use the comment to say something the code alone does not already convey.

coverageGaps: PEP 8/257 say nothing about is_/has_ prefixes for boolean variables or methods, unlike some other community style guides — no boolean_variable rule was included since none is actually stated.
PEP 8 defines no interface-naming convention (e.g. Java's Runnable or C#'s 'I' prefix), since Python has no first-class interface construct.
PEP 8 gives no enum-member casing rule distinct from the general constant convention (Java/C# often specify ALL_CAPS or PascalCase enum members explicitly).
PEP 8 gives no acronym-casing rule for CapWords/PascalCase identifiers (e.g. whether 'HTTPServer' or 'HttpServer' is preferred), unlike some Java/C# guides.
PEP 8 defines no minimum/maximum identifier-length rule, unlike some enterprise Java/C# style guides.

PEP 8 does define a Type Variable naming convention (CapWords, short names like T/AnyStr, with _co/_contra suffixes for variance) but it has no slot in the given identifierKind set (no 'type_parameter' kind), so it could not be represented as a NamingRule here.

Neither PEP 8 nor PEP 257 mandates a required docstring markup format (no enforced Google-style Args/Returns, NumPy-style, or reST field list) — tooling that expects one is layering an external convention (e.g. Google or NumPy docstring style guides) on top of PEP 8/257, not enforcing PEP 8 itself.
